title: Paranormal Investigator to host 'Haunted Mare Island'

content:
Jeffrey Dwyer, Ph.D., a professional paranormal investigator and acclaimed author, has set his sights on Mare Island this spooky season.

Dwyer will return to Mare Island’s St. Peter’s Chapel on Saturday to lead the Mare Island Historic Park Foundation’s (MIHPF) Speaker Series presentation, “Haunted Mare Island.” The event will explore eerie local legends, reported paranormal encounters, and unexplained phenomena from Mare Island and throughout the San Francisco Bay Area.

Dwyer has authored a 10-book series of nonfiction city history guides, along with five textbooks on paranormal subjects. He has appeared on more than 100 radio programs and on television, including big-name programs on the Discovery and Travel channels.

A frequent guest on Bay Area radio and television programs, Dwyer’s career has also set him up to present to audiences of up to 2,000 people and to cover topics ranging from paranormal phenomena to medical research.

His interest in the unexplained has taken him throughout the Bay Area, and on that map, part of his interests includes Mare Island. MIHPF organizers describe Dwyer as “not only a seasoned investigator but also an accomplished public speaker.”

“He conducted an additional paranormal investigation of the Admiral’s Mansion on Mare Island recently, and he’s going to reveal some of those interesting findings at this year’s presentation,” said Dennis Kelly, a member of the MIHPF board of directors.

According to Kelly, this will be Dwyer’s third year leading the presentation, which has nearly sold out each time it has been held.

The event, held in conjunction with Halloween, typically attracts a range of spectators each year. The crowd, Kelly says, is generally made up of half skeptics and half who are completely sold on the whole idea of paranormal experiences.”

Either way, attendees always have a good time.

The crowd dresses up in Halloween costumes, and “everybody has a lot of fun, no matter where they sit on the spectrum,” he said.

Without giving away too much, Kelly says one of the presentation’s recurring topics is the haunting legend of Lieutenant Commander Samuel Wilson, whose story has become part of Mare Island’s paranormal lore.

As the story goes, Wilson was serving as the executive officer on board USS “Ashuelot” in the U.S. Navy’s Asiatic Station. After suffering an epileptic fit, he died and was buried with military honors in Japan.

Three years later, his body was exhumed — for unknown reasons — and brought back for burial at Mare Island.

“They dug up his body and sent it to Mare Island on a sailing ship to be buried in the Mare Island cemetery,” explained Kelly, “but when the ship arrived here, it got decommissioned, and the boxes with the body got left in this building and were forgotten for years.”

In search of her deceased husband’s body years later, the story follows Wilson’s ex-wife, who came to Mare Island, only to find that the body was unable to be found.

“There are people who, because of it, swear that the building is haunted, even to the point where when the shipyard was still open, the people who worked in the building insisted that the lights be left on night and day,” said Kelly. “And they were for a number of years.”

The “Haunted Mare Island” presentation will take place from 3 to 4 p.m. Saturday at St. Peter’s Chapel on Mare Island.

Advance tickets start at $15, while tickets purchased at the door are $20, subject to availability. For event information and tickets, visit the MIHPF ticket page.
